blocks.markdown: The **policy of insurance** is the written instrument in which a contract of insurance is set forth. Read it together with valid riders, endorsements, applicable law, and any application made part of the contract.

How to read an insurance policy in a problem question: **(1)** identify the parties — insurer, insured, policyholder, beneficiary, and any mortgagee or other interested person; **(2)** identify the insured interest — person/life/health, property, liability, or a suretyship obligation; **(3)** identify the risk covered and the period when coverage applies, comparing loss date with effective and expiration dates; **(4)** look for exclusions, conditions, notices, limits, deductibles, endorsements, and applicable statutory rules; **(5)** check payment — premium receipt, grace period, credited premium, broker/agent collection, and whether statutory exceptions apply; **(6)** for property insurance, ask whether the claimant had insurable interest when coverage took effect and when the loss occurred; **(7)** for more than one policy, distinguish double insurance from overinsurance and avoid awarding more than the amount legally recoverable.

blocks.markdown: Content and form of the policy

An insurance policy can be printed or electronic. Attached clauses must be properly identified in the policy, and a rider added after issuance generally needs the insured's or owner's countersignature unless they applied for it. A hidden or improperly incorporated rider may not bind the insured.

Treat Section 51 as the policy checklist: parties, amount, premium or premium basis, property or life covered, interest in the property, covered risks, and duration. Some open or running policies do not state a fixed insured amount in the ordinary way.
Riders

A rider adds, removes, or changes policy terms — for example, an exclusion or extra benefit. Two separate questions matter: was the rider form approved by the Insurance Commissioner, and was it properly incorporated into the policy under Section 50?

**Exam point.** A rider does not automatically bind the insured merely because a copy is physically attached. Check the statutory formalities and whether the insured or owner agreed to a rider added after issuance.
Cover notes

A cover note is temporary evidence that insurance has been bound while the formal policy is being prepared. Under the statutory text, the formal policy should be issued within 60 days. Extension past that period is controlled by the Code and Insurance Commission rules.
Types of non-life policies

blocks.markdown: Parties: the insurer

A person or entity cannot simply call itself an insurer; it must fall within the permitted entity forms and have the authority required by the Insurance Code. The entity must be acting as principal in the insurance business, and the section distinguishes domestic from foreign companies and specifically addresses professional reinsurers.
Agents and brokers

A broker assists the insured in obtaining insurance; an agent acts on behalf of the insurer. The practical roles can overlap in ordinary speech, but the Code uses distinct legal definitions. The Code classifies the agent as an independent contractor, though the insurer may supervise agent activities under Insurance Commission rules because insurance affects the public. Licensing rules also apply; Section 307 is the related licensing provision.
Parties: the insured
One co-owner does not automatically insure every other co-owner's interest. The wording of the policy must extend to the joint or common interest.

**Trap.** The policy can be written to follow the insured interest to a later owner, but the policy must be framed that way. Do not assume every transfer of property automatically transfers its insurance; see Section 58.

table.caption: Part 1 review: core distinctions
rows: Life vs. property insurance
Life policy usually pays the amount fixed in the contract (Section 186); property insurance generally indemnifies the insured for covered loss within the policy and law.
Individual vs. group life
Individual policy covers an individual under a personal policy; group life uses a master policy covering eligible members of a group and has specific statutory provisions under Section 234.
Marine vs. fire vs. casualty

Marine: navigation, transit, transportation, cargo and related liabilities. Fire: fire and covered allied perils. Casualty: accident or mishap losses/liabilities not treated exclusively as another insurance class.
Suretyship
Surety guarantees the principal/obligor’s performance to the obligee, within the terms and cap of the bond.
Insurable interest in life vs. property
Life/health interest must exist when the policy takes effect; property interest must exist both when the insurance takes effect and when loss occurs (Section 19).
Double insurance vs. overinsurance
Double insurance is multiple policies on the same subject and interest; overinsurance is coverage exceeding insurable value. The concepts overlap but are not identical.
Sections 77 and 79
Section 77 states the general premium-payment rule and exceptions; Section 79 makes an acknowledgment in the policy or premium receipt conclusive evidence of payment for the purpose stated.
Cancellation vs. renewal
Section 64 (with Section 65 notice rules) governs cancellation of non-life policies; Section 66 governs notice of intention not to renew or to reduce/eliminate coverage.
Lapse vs. reinstatement
A lapsed life policy may be reinstated only if conditions in Section 233(j) and the policy are met. It is not the same as an automatic revival without payment or evidence of insurability.
